title: 414. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Trigonometric Signs by Quadrant
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Signs of sine and cosine in Quadrant II
questions.learningObjective: State the signs of sine and cosine for an angle in Quadrant II.
questions.question: The terminal side of \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant II. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate and \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate. In Quadrant II, \(x<0\) and \(y>0\), so \(\sin\theta>0\) and \(\cos\theta<0\). Both are negative only in Quadrant III.
questions.hint: Think of the signs of the \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates in that quadrant.

questions.concept: Sign of tangent in Quadrant III
questions.learningObjective: Determine the sign of tangent from the signs of sine and cosine.
questions.question: The terminal side of \(\theta\) lies in Quadrant III. What is the sign of \(\tan\theta\)?
questions.explanation: In Quadrant III both \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) are negative. Since \(\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), the quotient of two negative numbers is positive. Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV, where sine and cosine have opposite signs.
questions.hint: Write tangent as sine divided by cosine and use the sign of each.

questions.concept: Quadrant from the signs of sine and cosine
questions.learningObjective: Identify the quadrant of an angle from the signs of its sine and cosine.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\sin\theta<0\) and \(\cos\theta>0\). In which quadrant does its terminal side lie?
questions.explanation: A positive cosine means a positive \(x\)-coordinate (Quadrant I or IV). A negative sine means a negative \(y\)-coordinate (Quadrant III or IV). Both conditions hold only in Quadrant IV. In Quadrant II the signs are the reverse.
questions.hint: Translate each inequality into the sign of a coordinate of a point on the unit circle.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the sign of the cosine of a given angle in degrees.
questions.question: What is the sign of \(\cos 200^\circ\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(180^\circ<200^\circ<270^\circ\), the terminal side is in Quadrant III, where the \(x\)-coordinate is negative. Hence \(\cos 200^\circ<0\); in fact \(\cos 200^\circ=-\cos 20^\circ\approx -0.94\).
questions.hint: Locate the quadrant of the angle first.

questions.concept: Quadrant from the signs of tangent and sine
questions.learningObjective: Identify the quadrant of an angle from the signs of its tangent and sine.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan\theta<0\) and \(\sin\theta>0\). In which quadrant does its terminal side lie?
questions.explanation: A positive sine occurs in Quadrants I and II. A negative tangent occurs where sine and cosine have opposite signs, in Quadrants II and IV. The only quadrant satisfying both conditions is Quadrant II. In Quadrant IV the sine is negative.
questions.hint: List the quadrants allowed by each condition and take the one they share.

questions.concept: Sign of the sine of a negative angle
questions.learningObjective: Determine the sign of a sine value for a negative angle.
questions.question: What is the sign of \(\sin(-100^\circ)\)?
questions.explanation: The angle \(-100^\circ\) is measured clockwise and is coterminal with \(260^\circ\), which is in Quadrant III. There the \(y\)-coordinate is negative, so \(\sin(-100^\circ)<0\). Although \(\sin 100^\circ\) is positive, the sign changes for the negative angle.
questions.hint: Find a positive coterminal angle and locate its quadrant.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the quadrant of an angle from the signs of cotangent and secant.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\cot\theta>0\) and \(\sec\theta<0\). In which quadrant does its terminal side lie?
questions.explanation: A reciprocal has the same sign as the original function. So \(\tan\theta>0\), which occurs in Quadrants I and III, and \(\cos\theta<0\), which occurs in Quadrants II and III. Both hold only in Quadrant III. In Quadrant I every trigonometric function is positive, so \(\sec\theta<0\) fails.
questions.hint: Replace each reciprocal function by the basic function with the same sign.

questions.concept: Sign of a product of sine and cosine
questions.learningObjective: Determine the quadrants in which a product of two trigonometric values is positive.
questions.question: In which quadrants is the product \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\) positive?
questions.explanation: A product is positive when its factors have the same sign. Sine and cosine are both positive in Quadrant I and both negative in Quadrant III. In Quadrant II the sine is positive and the cosine is negative, so the product is negative there.
questions.hint: A product of two numbers is positive exactly when the numbers have the same sign.

questions.concept: Sign of a product at two angles
questions.learningObjective: Combine the signs of two trigonometric values at different angles.
questions.question: What is the sign of \(\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}\cdot\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}\)?
questions.explanation: The angle \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) is in Quadrant IV, where tangent is negative. The angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) is in Quadrant II, where cosine is negative. The product of two negative numbers is positive. Exactly, \(\left(-\sqrt{3}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
questions.hint: Find the quadrant and sign for each factor separately, then multiply the signs.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the signs of sine and cosine of half of a second-quadrant angle.
questions.question: Suppose \(90^\circ<\theta<180^\circ\). Which statement about \(\frac{\theta}{2}\) is correct?
questions.explanation: Dividing the inequality by \(2\) gives \(45^\circ<\frac{\theta}{2}<90^\circ\), so \(\frac{\theta}{2}\) lies in Quadrant I. There both sine and cosine are positive. The signs of \(\theta\) itself (sine positive, cosine negative) do not carry over to \(\frac{\theta}{2}\).
questions.hint: Divide every part of the inequality for \(\theta\) by \(2\) to locate \(\frac{\theta}{2}\).
